title: Milestones – 1956 portraits and life stories in the Hungarian emigration in America

stories.name: András Farkas
paragraphs: His father was a disabled veteran of the First World War who worked as a tobacconist from the nineteen-thirties until the early fifties. The communist takeover radically changed the family’s life.
After elementary school András Farkas trained as a motorcycle and car mechanic, and became a racing cyclist.
During the days of the revolution he took photographs and travelled around the country by bicycle.
“Before Fehérvár I said this is not good, we got off, and went on by bicycle. Two days earlier I had won the Budapest championship; I was a road racer. Cycling was nothing to me.”
After the revolution was crushed he left Hungary. He continued his life in emigration as a photographer and a sportsman.
And what became of the 1956 photographs, the reason he left Hungary? His younger brother, who stayed at home and would have had something to fear, burned the negatives.

stories.name: Klára Aich
paragraphs: She was born in Budapest in 1943 into an intellectual and factory-owning family. In 1951 the family was deported to Visonta. “Children, be glad, we are going to the countryside,” said Klára’s father cheerfully — he had been managing director of the Dreher Brewery, and a gentleman remains a gentleman even in hell. Although the deportation was dramatic for her parents, for Klára it passed happily. The family was housed with a kulak.

“The people of Visonta were very kind. They invited us to a wedding and sat me next to the bride, as an important guest. They respected us. But you could not leave the village. They came in at night and shone lights on the beds to see whether everyone was there. There was no doctor in the village. Once my mother had to go to a dentist in Gyöngyös. We were terrified; if she had been seen, they could have taken her to prison. There were such cases. But two and a half years of growing up in a village… we were much freer. I cannot say a single bad thing about it, I only saw that it was hard for my parents. My parents were so extraordinary that they expressed no problem in front of the children, they did not quarrel, they named no names — I am grateful to them for that. It was a carefree time.”

In 1953 the family moved to Solymár, because deported families were not allowed to move to a large city. Her mother became a translator, her father a doorman at the Astoria. In 1955 the secret police took her father away.

“At night in Solymár the whole family sat waiting for my father to come home on the last bus. Then there was a knock and three secret policemen came in. They asked where my father was. They set to and searched the house. They threw the whole flat about. When they had finished they told us to sit down and wait for my father. I shall never forget it. It was shattering. We sat there in the dark kitchen with the secret policemen, in silence. Nobody spoke. We waited for my father to come home. My father came home. He saw the secret policemen sitting in the dark. I saw the terror in his face. They took him away because he had copied out a poem. He had a friend who wrote an anti-communist poem, and he copied it. For months we did not know where he was. He was in the political prison. He did not say much about it.”
The family lived through the revolution in Solymár. Her parents did not want to cross the border with two daughters.

“In December my father set off, meaning to go alone and bring the family out later. I remember saying goodbye; we did not really understand what was happening. My uncle worked for the Zöldért company. He was able to give my father a docket to deliver vegetables to the border. The lorry was full of refugees, and the driver informed on them. They were all arrested. He spent ten days in custody. He swallowed the addresses. He was carrying a great many foreign addresses from the brewery.”

“A law came out, it lasted only a very short time, but we fell within it. Anyone over fifty-five, or a girl under sixteen, who had a country willing to invite them, could leave. My father was fifty-eight, we were under sixteen. We received an invitation from the Netherlands saying they would help us leave the country, but we could not go to the Netherlands. The family left with one suitcase each. Two weeks later the law was withdrawn. The law existed because so many had left that a great many children and parents were left behind, for whom the state was responsible.”

“We set off. We did not know where to. We had a twenty-four-hour transit permit through Austria, but we had no receiving country and we were not refugees. My parents set off with two children and four suitcases and nowhere to go, only the hope that somehow it would be arranged. There was no relief organisation of any kind behind us.”

Klára’s father had been a hussar ensign in the First World War. In Vienna a former comrade from the war took the family in. The Dreher family placed the two sisters in a convent, and Klára went on to study photography. In 1965, without her parents’ consent, she moved to New York to become a photographer; her sister settled in Greece.
“They left because of us, and in the end they were left alone. That was very sad. That is emigration. I do not recommend it to everyone. People fall apart, families fall apart.”

Klára Aich built a successful career as a photographer in New York, opened her own studio and began working for the largest fashion houses while mounting numerous exhibitions. Her Manhattan studio-home remains to this day a meeting place for musicians, visual artists and lovers of art.

stories.name: Csaba Téglás
paragraphs: He was born in Kecskemét in 1930 but spent his childhood in Újszász in ideal rural circumstances. The Second World War and the communist turn that followed it fundamentally changed his life.
At the time of the 1956 revolution he was living and working in Budapest. After the revolution was crushed he left Hungary.

He arrived in Canada in 1957 and moved to America in 1967. In 1998 his book appeared in English: Budapest Exit, a memoir dealing with the history of the Second World War, the Holocaust, the 1956 revolution and emigration.

stories.name: Zoltán and Judit Szántó
paragraphs: He was born in Berettyóújfalu in 1935 into a landowning family that lived from agriculture. His father went missing in the Second World War and his mother died after it. He studied at a building-construction technical school in Debrecen, but spent a year in a lung sanatorium being treated for a pulmonary infection.

“So my whole life began badly… I went up to Budapest after 4 November. My mother’s brother’s children were there… One of their sons, Dezső Sápi, was shot on Kossuth Square and died. Of course the family searched everywhere; the circumstances were very sad. My other cousin and I decided to try somehow to get abroad. By then it was 23 November. The borders had already been closed. We took the train to Szombathely; there were a lot of young lads on the train, and one of them lived in Szombathely. He offered to let us go to their house and sleep there, which was a great thing. The next day we had breakfast and set off for the border. There was a guide, to whom I gave my money and my camera. They said the border was already closed and that we should not hurry — that we should go once it was dark. On 23 November it was already cold. Ploughed fields, maize, puddles. If we went quietly, perhaps we could get across. Suddenly they began firing flares. Of course everyone threw themselves down. We crawled like snakes. Somehow I managed to crawl a good distance out. With a few other lads I went to a spot where there was a small hut and some straw stacks. We slept. The next morning more lads arrived from elsewhere. How to get across? The water in the river was high, you could not simply wade through in the cold. We found a boat, moored. Three or four of us crossed, then one rowed back and brought the others. My cousin was left behind somewhere. He was shot, then caught, and given two years in prison. His mother later lost her mind. One of her sons had been shot dead, the other imprisoned.”

After the border crossing the refugees were taken by lorry to Graz. There they were given food and pocket money, and it was recorded where each wished to go. The quota for America was already full, so Szántó ended up in Germany. There he met his wife, Judit, herself a 1956 émigré. ‘What a pity this boy is German,’ Judit said. Eleven days later they were married, and together they applied for Canada, where in the end they did not go. They were given a temporary flat in Munich and both enrolled to study architecture at the university. In 1962 a new quota opened for America; doctors and engineers could come.

“We came out on a military aircraft, a four-engine one. There were a lot of little babies on the plane. Children of American soldiers who had been adopted by Americans. Constant crying the whole way. We reached the English Channel and one of the engines caught fire. There was an emergency landing in Ireland.”
The International Rescue Committee was waiting for them at the airport. Szántó worked as an engineer at several companies, then founded his own firm together with two fellow 1956 émigrés.

He is an active member of the American Hungarian Memorial Committee, whose decade of work resulted in the erection of the 1956 memorial in New York. The construction drawings for the New York 1956 memorial were made in the Szántós’ basement. Zoltán and Judit are also major donors to the 1956 memorial erected in Passaic in 1989.

stories.name: István Lakatos
paragraphs: István Lakatos lived through the Second World War in Dunapataj and Budapest. Many defining, traumatic experiences are bound to that period. After the war the family returned to Szeged, where his father worked as a teacher. István Lakatos went to university to read geography and geology, and the outbreak of the revolution found him working as a teaching assistant.
His father had a large library, including anti-communist volumes. A raid reached them too, but miraculously only one book was taken.
“Then my father said: ‘son, where books are burned, there will be dictatorship’.”

The young assistant could barely fend off pressure to join the party, pleading his ideological inadequacy. In the end, once he had been threatened that without joining he could not remain an assistant, he prepared to change jobs. But the revolution intervened, with the ever more serious meetings of the Szeged students, in the course of which MEFESZ — the Union of Hungarian University and College Students’ Associations, replacing the communist DISZ — was founded. By then he was courting a girl named Magdi.
“The revolution began in Szeged with the founding of MEFESZ, and on the twenty-third the emphasis shifted to Budapest.”
In response to the brutality of the armed forces a National Guard was founded in Szeged. István Lakatos became deputy commander of its rapid unit.

“We took up firing positions opposite the secret police barracks and sent our commander out to the sentry to say that members of the National Guard were here and wanted to speak to the commanding officer. He said this was a military barracks and one could not simply come in. Our commander, Jóska Kendi, was a wrestler; he seized him, took the submachine gun off him and said, now you run up and tell them we are coming up — and he was already going after him. We were lucky, because more than a hundred secret policemen lived there, but they were just then withdrawing. We came by a lot of weapons; they did not want a fight. We said we would shoot, but they had the advantage — they could have wiped us out.”

After the defeat of the revolution he escaped to Yugoslavia and spent five months in a refugee camp before he could go to Canada. He worked in a car factory, washed cars and washed dishes in a restaurant, then was able to finish university in geology. After that he started work, and wanted only to bring his love to Canada. Magdi was allowed out with a tourist group to the Rome Olympics, and István went into action. He travelled to Rome and, with the help of a priest he knew there, tracked Magdi down, going from hotel to hotel.

“The morning of the fifth day came. I learned afterwards that Magdi’s group would have set off home on the morning of the sixth. On the morning of the fifth day I went into a hotel and showed the porter Magdi’s photograph. He said, she is here, but they have gone on an excursion to Naples. Opposite the hotel there was a small restaurant; I sat down at the tables on the pavement and ordered a glass of beer. And what does God give me — the tourist coach really did pull in, and among the first to get off was Magdi. And our eyes met. I turned my gaze away, signalling that this was all I could do, now you must do something. Then Magdi, as she told me later, came to her senses, gave her bag to one of her companions to take up to her room, and said she was going to buy some fruit at the greengrocer next door. I stood up, and we walked in parallel on the two sides of the street. Magdi looked back at the corner; people stood frozen like pillars of salt, watching what was happening. They did not grasp it at all. We began to run, one corner this way, the next corner that way. Then we jumped into a taxi.”

The Vatican would gladly have married them, but without baptismal certificates it could not be done. They went up to San Marino, but the only notary there was on holiday. On their return incredible news awaited them.

“And then Ottó appeared, crying out: children, there is a God in heaven! To hear that from a priest… Imagine, copies of your baptismal certificates have arrived from Hungary at the Vatican! The Vatican never told us how, since there were no diplomatic relations, but they obtained the papers. We understand it was arranged through the Swedish embassy. We found two witnesses, a medical student and the oldest Hungarian in Rome. When we came out of the Chapel of St Anne after the ceremony, reporters were standing there with cameras, and the paper carried our story — we do not know how they found out.”
Two weeks later Magdi landed in Canada.

István Lakatos is professor emeritus at the City University of New York and founding chairman of the American Hungarian Memorial Committee, whose decade of work resulted in the erection of the 1956 memorial in New York.

stories.name: György Lovas
paragraphs: He was born in Budapest in 1931 into a merchant family from Losonc. He lived through the Second World War and the Holocaust as a child. His parents died of tuberculosis; in 1944 his grandparents were loaded into wagons by the Germans and taken from the Losonc ghetto. He came alone to relatives in Pest. Already in his grammar-school years he edited a student paper.

“Before my final exams the paper was shut down and I was summoned to the district committee of DISZ, the Union of Working Youth. They told me that if I remained a reactionary I would have no future, but that if I attended the district committee a serious career awaited me. But I did not want that career.”

He was conscripted, but because of a forgery committed in the army he was locked up immediately after demobilisation and spent eleven months in the Csillag prison in Szeged. After his release he took work at the shipyard in Újpest, where he organised musical gatherings and played drums in the band.

“That is how it went until 23 October, which fell on a Tuesday. I shall never forget it, because we had band rehearsal every Tuesday. I worked only four hours that day and hurried to rehearsal, but I heard that there was a demonstration at the Bem statue. Crowds were coming over from Buda to the Parliament. We threw everything aside and caught the last trams still running into the city. We joined the crowd at the Margaret Bridge. From that moment I did not see another suit until I crossed the Austrian border.”
György Lovas threw himself straight into the thick of events and tried to obtain weapons for the revolutionaries.

“A lorry was going towards Vác for food; three of us climbed onto it, and it dropped us on Váci Road at the entrance to the Újpest shipyard. The guard let us in; we said we had left our bags there. We broke a padlock and brought out pistols. The guards were with us at once. A Russian military Skoda came along and asked where we were going; I said into town. We got in. From behind, the others shot the major and the driver dead. We loaded up the submachine guns and raced into the city in the Skoda.”

After 4 November the men in Újpest gave up the fight; they saw no sense in further bloodshed. Lovas did not stop until New York, where he went into business and worked as a journalist, took a leading role in several associations of revolutionaries and was present at numerous protests against communist oppression.

“In April 1957 I cut down the communist Hungarian flag in front of the United Nations. Antal Kiss and Laci Tóth were there; the first had been a journalist at Magyar Hírlap, the second an MTI photographer who had escaped. We went to the UN at ten in the morning and I saw the flag with the hammer and sickle, the one we had torn out during the revolution. Antal said, leave it, what do you want? We have to put the paper together! We were on our way to the printer with Szabad Magyarság. I took matters into my own hands — I had a pocket knife — climbed the wall, and Laci Tóth photographed it. I cut the flag down, spat on it, tore it to pieces, and then the police came. That was the first flag-tearing at the UN; afterwards the Arabs and others followed me. But I was the first. And at the police station we shouted that wherever we saw that flag we would tear it down, and that we would ask everyone who saw it anywhere to tear it down! That flag does not represent Hungary! The entire world press picked it up; the next day there were three pictures of me in the New York Times, six in all. Life magazine had the whole thing across its centre. Everyone carried it, Paris, London. I wanted it to go out into the world. The aim of the World Federation of Freedom Fighters was that we should not let the memory of the revolution be lulled to sleep, that it should remain in the memory of every child, every adult and every old woman!”

Over the past six decades György Lovas has been an outstanding figure of 1956-related programmes and events across America. He was chief organiser of the commemorative gala held at Carnegie Hall on the fiftieth anniversary of the revolution. Since 2006 he has been an active member of the American Hungarian Memorial Committee, whose decade of work resulted in the erection of the 1956 memorial in New York.

stories.name: Erzsébet Molnár-Rajec
paragraphs: She was born into a family of small artisans in Pozsony. Her father had a flourishing tailoring business with employees and apprentices. The historical changes and the communist system fundamentally transformed their family’s life as well.
Erzsébet lived through the events of 1956 in Budapest.
“I was sitting with Marianne Csernus on Stalin Avenue, in the Eszpresszó café. Suddenly Gerő’s speech comes over the radio, and everything changed.”
After the revolution was crushed she set off for the border with her family. The escape was especially hard with a nine-month-old child.

“We had to cross. The water was the dividing wall. Nobody wanted to come with us, because we had a nine-month-old baby with us. I was left alone with the family; they were afraid the baby’s voice would give us away. We were given instructions that if we heard the tanks, we should keep silent.”
In emigration she did literary and community work, and preserved the memory of 1956.

stories.name: Iván Bódis-Wollner
paragraphs: He lived through the Holocaust as a small child: his family was taken to the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, where his grandfather taught him to read and write — and where relativity theory and the stars were also part of the “curriculum”.

“I caught measles in the camp and was moved to a children’s hospital where there were two beds. There was a little girl next to me, which made me very happy. I was given milk, which had frozen by morning. My mother, my father and my grandmother did not know where I was. One of the camp guards, a Hungarian Swabian, stole my mother out one night and brought her in to me. Then he stole her back. He was gambling with his life.”

“The British liberated the camp, and the Germans, who were in the process of losing the war, put the Hungarians on a train and shipped us east. We wandered away from the railway into the surrounding villages and begged for food. The poor Germans had no food themselves, but they gave us some. As a gesture that mattered enormously. To us, and to them. Just as it mattered that when we were first loaded into wagons in 1944, in great heat, people came and tried to give us water.”

“Later, under communism, when I had to prove that I was not a class enemy — which of course I was — I worked every summer. One year I weeded for the municipal gardens on Mechwart Square and enjoyed myself thoroughly, which apparently displeased somebody, because afterwards they sent me out towards Hűvösvölgy, where prisoners were building a road. My job was to carry water. I remember clearly that the road they were building was not entirely precise. I said to one of the men that it was not straight. He looked at me and said: you know, I was not brought up to build roads. He was a Count Batthyány.”

“In the meantime I was reclassified from class enemy to ‘intellectual — other’, because my father was a doctor, so I was admitted to the university in Szeged. I had originally wanted to work in number theory, but there was no place for that, and my father wanted me to become a doctor, so a medical student is what I became.”

He played bridge regularly with his friends and was present at those meetings of Szeged students where the revolutionary demands were formulated, and at one of which MEFESZ, the Union of Hungarian University and College Students’ Associations, was founded.
“Paradoxically, it was thanks to the regime that we knew Russian and knew how to argue with Marxists.”
He joined the National Guard and was a leading figure at numerous demonstrations.

“On the evening of 4 November we went out to the bridge, where with a Second World War submachine gun we resolved to fire on the Russian tanks. Thank God we did not fire; the Russian tanks did not look like anything a shot would have troubled. So we did not fire. There were six or seven of us there on the bank of the Tisza.”

On his mother’s advice he went to Yugoslavia, where he stayed with relatives in Subotica, then moved to Vienna and enrolled at the university. Until he received a scholarship he worked in a chocolate factory. Later he passed through many universities, studying among others at the Sorbonne in Paris, at Cornell in the United States, and in Cambridge, Bristol and Edinburgh.
He lives in Brooklyn, New York City, and is professor of neurology at SUNY Downstate Medical Center and a world-renowned researcher of Parkinson’s disease.

stories.name: Éva Bálintitt
paragraphs: A scion of a Transylvanian aristocratic family, she was nevertheless born in Budapest in 1935. Her father was Baron István Apor of Altorja, a ministerial counsellor at the prime minister’s office. After the war István Apor was placed on the B-list, then pensioned off at fifty-five, and finally his pension was taken away too. The family lived on what Éva earned as a fourteen-year-old delivery girl for a flower shop. A relative of the family was Vilmos Apor, bishop of Győr, who was shot dead for protecting women from Russian soldiers. Éva Bálintitt was present at the bishop’s beatification. Her father’s brother was Gábor Apor, ambassador to the Holy See. Éva Bálintitt was confirmed by Cardinal-Primate József Mindszenty in St Stephen’s Basilica.

The family lived through the siege of Budapest in the cellar of their block; their mother lost her life during the bombing. Éva first attended the Mrs Miklós Horthy Girls’ Home, then the school of the Sisters of the Sacred Heart, but in the communist years she was not permitted to continue her studies, as a class enemy. She earned her living as a technical draughtswoman and cartographer. She spent several years in Balmazújváros, where she worked as a surveyor.
Éva met her future husband, Károly Bálintitt, at a party given by her godfather Sándor Teleki. The couple were married by Mihály Endrey, auxiliary bishop of Vác, in the University Church in Budapest.
“Somebody at the wedding said, I see a thousand years of prison here! There were people in Hungarian ceremonial dress under communism, and the street had to be closed because of the crowd!”

Károly Bálintitt was a Transylvanian aristocrat, heir to the castle at Nagyernye not far from Marosvásárhely. Among other things he served as military attaché in Ankara. At the beginning of communism he tried to escape to the West, but was caught at the border and spent time in prison.
Asked how the aristocracy experienced communism, Éva answers:
“Proudly, because they wanted to humiliate everyone, but they found no wailing aristocrats. Everyone bore it as though this were what had now been dealt to us.”
In 1956 Éva and her husband were at the demonstration on Kossuth Square. They were standing by the Ministry of Agriculture.

“Suddenly a tank moved off to the left, then they began shooting; Charlie pushed me behind the arcades, and we saw the bullets ricocheting off the ground. Charlie climbed over the backs of the crowd and pushed me in through a ministry window that was open. There was a group of people inside; we jumped out of a window on the other side, my ankle turned, but a doctor passing by set it right. Then a crowd in black came, perhaps a hundred people, with a black flag and a Hungarian flag with a hole in the middle. We ended up in Váci Street, where music was playing from the espresso bar and chatter could be heard — they knew nothing about any of it.”
They set off westwards on 21 November 1956.

“The plan was to leave on the nineteenth, together with a couple who were friends, but Charlie did not feel like getting up, since the rain was pouring, and he said we should not go. Over the next two days he sank into such lethargy that when they called from outside, he wanted to go after all. He arranged it with Gábor Zichy, who arrived with an enormous rucksack; I said, Charlie, that has ‘escaping’ written all over it, let us not go with him.”

They went by train as far as Győr, then by taxi to the border, from where a three-and-a-half-hour walk brought them into Austria. There, thanks to the Order of Malta, they slept in a school on straw laid on the floor.

In Vienna Károly Bálintitt worked for the International Committee for European Migration. That organisation distributed people. In the end the Bálintitts too moved to America. Éva found work as a cartographer and works to this day. Károly Bálintitt was given a job as a translator at Bank of America, and after being pensioned off at sixty-five took a post at his cousin’s import-export firm, which operated on the eighty-third floor of the World Trade Center. The owner died, and his wife wound up the company six weeks before the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001.
Had she not done so, they would have been working in that office that day too. Károly Bálintitt went on working from his own home and died at the age of 103.

The family reclaimed the castle at Nagyernye and its estate, whose affairs are managed by their son, Charlie Bálintitt Jr. For many decades Éva has been one of the defining figures and chief organisers of Hungarian social life in New York, of the Transylvanian Tea Evenings and the bridge parties.

stories.name: György Mismás
paragraphs: He was born into a peasant family sometime in the winter of 1934 in Murarátka, but the day of his christening became his birthday. His father bought a tavern in the village, for which he was classified a kulak, and the family was deported to the Hortobágy.

“On 7 June 1950 secret policemen appeared. They came in armed; my father was not at home, and my brother had to sign a paper saying that we would not resist and that we were to be deported. They gave us an hour to pack and took us away on a lorry, and then we travelled by train for two nights and a day.”
They spent years in a stable, crammed together in inhuman conditions.

“Two people could dress between the beds. We lived together, we slept together; there was no shame there — if you had to undress, you undressed. A little girl was washing her face in the bucket one morning and showed me her breasts. We lived like animals for thirty-nine months.”
The deported were made to do heavy physical work, chiefly in agriculture.

“The hardest was lifting beet. For eight hours you had to bend down and pull up the beet. Behind one of the maize fields ran a canal, and three of us children went in after work to cool off. We were punished. They took us to the police station, and you had to lean against the wall standing half a metre from it, your hands tied behind you, propping the wall up with your forehead. We had to stand like that for two and a half hours. First your legs tremble, then later you slide down. You tore the skin off your forehead. They sluiced you with water and carried on.”
Later György Mismás went to work in a factory in Csepel, but former deportees were forbidden to live in large cities.

During the revolution Mismás reinforced the fighters of Corvin Passage. He was also present at the battle on Köztársaság Square, where the communist party headquarters was fired on from the roof of the Erkel Theatre.

“I was up on the theatre roof with a mate who had a machine gun. I fed the rounds, I held the magazine. We fired into the second floor of the party building, because that is where we saw the secret police running about.”
György Mismás recounts his experiences of Corvin Passage thus:

“There was an occasion when a big Russian tank with a short gun came in and its track was shot away too, and I was standing at Nap Street; there were about twenty of us. They let off a smoke bomb. Within moments the smoke was such that I could not see my hand on the weapon. A strange thing happened: we are shooting, but we do not know at whom. A Russian officer came out of the smoke with a pistol. Somebody threw a grenade at him, and it exploded above him; his head burst apart, but he did not fall, he even went a few steps forward. And when he reached the pavement, then the poor man fell. In Práter Street there is a school; our command post was there. The saddest thing happened here. The upper floor was full of Russian soldiers who had surrendered. We had at least sixty to a hundred Russian prisoners. Next to us there was a hospital. A doctor from there who worked in it, still in his green clothes, had not seen his family for five days; he was coming down Nap Street, going home. On the other side of the street, on the second floor, a woman was standing with a small child in her arms. She was crying out with joy that at last here you are, you are alive! And he did not get home. He was shot dead.”

After the defeat of the revolution he crossed into Austria via the Rába canal. He spent three weeks in Vienna, then settled in America, where he first worked as a sheet-metal worker in a foundry. In 1967 he founded his own business in precision sheet-metal work. He is still active. He works for many large pharmaceutical companies, and several patents bear his name that assist the work of medicine, above all in making the detection of various cancers easier. György Mismás has sponsored numerous American and Hungarian memorials, films and books relating to 1956.

stories.name: László Papp
paragraphs: A descendant of a Debrecen burgher family; his father emigrated to Venezuela after the war, and his mother died very early. He enrolled at the Technical University in 1947.

“Until then the old professors were still there, the ones who were later thrown out of the university; they were respectable specialists from whom it was good to learn. The Technical University was a free-spirited place, but there were times when people disappeared, people were locked up, and one could not know what had happened to them. Before my final semester it was voted that I too should be expelled from the university. Thank God they threw me out — because those who graduated were called up as soldiers immediately. Anyone with a bad cadre record was assigned to labour service…”
In October 1956 he became chairman of the company revolutionary council at the Residential Building Design Company.

“I took part in a great many things. The events on Köztársaság Square, for example, were interesting. The party headquarters was on Köztársaság Square. The revolutionaries wanted to take the building, which was defended by the secret police. At the end of the siege there was an ugly incident; several secret policemen were lynched. After that a whole hysteria developed on the square. People believed they could hear captured people in underground prisons calling for help. Our office had designed that building. So I was asked, as chairman of the revolutionary council, to look into it. I had personal experience of how this worked, because our company designed the three villas in Buda in which Rákosi, Gerő and Mihály Farkas lived. Now, those really did have underground tunnels, but we did not design them; a department of the interior ministry did. We were given the connection drawing showing how the buildings we designed had to join onto them. So I knew what plans would have had to exist if the party headquarters had had to connect to similar underground facilities, if there had been underground bunkers. But I found none; there was no point of connection in the plans. So I saw it confirmed that this was only mass hysteria. And yet to this day it is an urban legend that there were underground prisons beneath Köztársaság Square.”
On 15 November, with a change of underwear, his diploma, a slide rule and a bottle of pálinka, they set off for the border.

“The train was packed with two kinds of people: one half were obviously city people fleeing. The other half were peasants who had gone into town to shop. It is an ingrained peasant conviction that if there is trouble one certainly will not be able to buy things, so let us buy what we can — and so they went into Győr. We went with empty bags. Then suddenly the train stopped in open country and three hundred people set off straight across the fields. There was no station, but the driver also knew what this was about. We were in the region of the Hanság marshes. We crossed by the marshy part.”
Since 2006 he has been a member of the American Hungarian Memorial Committee and is currently its chairman. The committee’s decade of work resulted in the erection of the 1956 memorial in New York.

stories.name: Balázs Somogyi
paragraphs: He was born in Győr in 1938. His father was a military doctor. He began his university studies six weeks before the outbreak of the revolution.
During the days of the revolution he took part in the demonstrations together with his fellow students, and after the Soviet intervention he set off westwards.
“The train was stopped at Győr. The railwaymen were on strike, we were stuck, we had to clamber down off the train and carry what could be carried. One difficult situation followed another.”
In the first years of emigration he did physical work.
“My first job: digging a ditch under the auspices of some electricity company. I very quickly realised that I am a clumsy ditch-digger.”
Later he continued his studies, entered medicine and built a career in America.

stories.name: István Gulyás
paragraphs: István Gulyás was born into a working-class family in Jászárokszállás in 1930. His studies and his work took him to Budapest.
At the time of the 1956 revolution he took an active part in events. He arranged his escape with his wife.
“I shall be at the Southern Railway Station; if you come, you come. I went home by hitchhiking. Telephoning was impossible. I did not know how to say what I meant — it was that dangerous.”
After the revolution was crushed he left the country.
István Gulyás arrived in America by ship, where he built a successful career as an architect and remained active in Hungarian community life.

stories.name: Béla Lipták
paragraphs: He was born in Budapest in 1936, but in his childhood the family lived at Furkópuszta in Tolna County. He studied at the Benedictine Grammar School in Pannonhalma, then went on to the Technical University.
In the period before the revolution he attended the meetings of the Petőfi Circle and took part in the formulation of the sixteen points at the Technical University.

“Then we realised that we all thought the same thing and that there was no need to be afraid of one another. After that we began to write the sixteen points — that evening only fourteen; the next day, on the way, we added the last two with the help of a teaching assistant named Jankovics.”
Béla Lipták fought in the area of Gellért Square and Móricz Zsigmond Circus. He was also in contact with Uncle Szabó, the leader of the insurgents at Széna Square.
During the fighting he watched a close friend die.

“With a submachine gun, in safety, behind the chestnut tree, and I cannot shoot. I am somehow made in such a way that I cannot shoot at a human being… I am ashamed of it to this day. Jancsi died partly because of me. There were twenty-seven bullets in his body.”

After the defeat of the revolution he fled to Austria and then to the United States. He worked as an engineer and university lecturer, and for many decades actively kept alive the memory of the 1956 revolution.

stories.name: Vilmos and Katalin Kovács
paragraphs: He was born in Budapest in 1937 into a family of skilled tradesmen and small entrepreneurs. He lived through the Second World War as a small boy in Csepel. His father was captured three times and three times escaped captivity. In 1951 his elder brother Lajos escaped to Yugoslavia.

“At that time Yugoslavia was not communist, but it was not the West either. They did not send him back, but they did not send him West either. They locked him up for five years. In ’56 they let him out. The revolution broke out; by then we knew he was already in Belgium. Because of that my father was interned for two years. At night five secret policemen came into the house; one of them held a pistol on my father while the other four searched the house completely. They took away every letter and photograph. They took my father away and did not say a single word to my mother about where they were taking him, why, or for how long. Nothing. Of course my mother fell ill. My other brother, Árpád, three years older than me, was at grammar school. He had to leave it and went to work at the Csepel Works. My father had a workshop, but the state took it over; they took everything. It took my mother six months to find out where my father was.”
In 1956, when the revolution broke out, Vilmos Kovács was working at Csepel. That evening he too, with his friend, was in front of the Parliament, and then they went to the Radio building.

“The square at the Radio building was full. We waited there to see what would happen. They told the people through loudspeakers that everyone should go home. Nobody moved, nobody went home. Then we heard shooting. I must have been about a hundred metres from the building, and my friend and I looked at each other. We thought they had fired into the air. Yes — but then three girls came running towards us covered in blood, and we looked at each other again. This cannot be. They are shooting at us, with live rounds they are shooting at us. We did not want to believe it.”
On 19 November Vilmos Kovács, his brother and two friends set off for the western border. They spent their last night in Hungary in the stable of a farm near Győr.

“We woke at four in the morning. The woman of the house gave each of us a sandwich. From four in the morning we walked all day, and there were more and more of us. There must have been a hundred and fifty. It almost looked as though we were walking home from a match at the People’s Stadium. Then suddenly we hear a lorry coming. It was full of secret police and Russian soldiers. A Hungarian soldier says through the megaphone: everyone come here, anyone who tries to run will be shot! There were people with children, families, young, old, all sorts. We walked slowly into the line so as not to be shot, but we did not hurry, so we ended up absolutely last. The line moved and I talked to the soldier, who had his rifle on his shoulder. I am nineteen, I said, next year I shall be a soldier too. I will not become a communist just because they put the uniform on me. You are not a communist either — let me go. He said nothing, rifle on his shoulder; I thought, then he certainly will not shoot me. I had just decided to jump into the bushes. At that moment I hear my brother saying, Vili, Vili! I look back, he was already in the bushes. We jumped in and waited for the line to pass. We tried to go towards Austria, but we kept hearing voices and footsteps. Refugees, of course. Within two hours there were fifty of us. It is interesting how at such times there is always somebody who takes the lead. We tried to read the trees to know where north was, which way to go. Twice we saw a light, but we almost went back to the Hungarian barracks. A third time we again see a moving light. It was a car. We start running in that direction. That was already Austria. The car stopped. He said, I am a doctor. I work by day and come at night to gather up the Hungarians. He gave us chocolate and oranges and took us to the collection point.”
In 1956 Vilmos Kovács and his brother Árpád Kovács came to Wallingford, Connecticut.

“The first morning my brother and I sat down. I said, we did not come here on holiday. We learned three hundred English words by heart. That gave us a head start over everyone else, because many could not even say ‘How are you?’”
In 1968 he and his brother founded their own tool-making and turning company, which grew into a successful business.

Vilmos Kovács and his wife, Katalin Kovács, have been active members of Hungarian community life in Connecticut from the beginning, and for several years ran the Hungarian Community House in Wallingford.
